Admissible Models for Compositional Data

Theory, Chapter 3

theory-03-admissible-models.Rmd

The constraint on models

The previous chapters established that cover data live on a constrained space: the simplex. A composition of KK components is a vector 𝐲=(y1,…,yK)\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \ldots, y_K) satisfying yk≥0y_k \geq 0 for all kk and ∑k=1Kyk=1\sum_{k=1}^{K} y_k = 1. This space is denoted 𝒮K−1\mathcal{S}^{K-1}, the (K−1)(K-1)-dimensional simplex embedded in ℝK\mathbb{R}^K.

Any probability model for cover data must assign probability only to points in this space. A distribution that places positive mass outside 𝒮K−1\mathcal{S}^{K-1} (on negative values, on values exceeding one, or on vectors that do not sum to one) is invalid. It describes a quantity other than the one measured.

This constraint must be satisfied before any other modelling consideration.

What admissibility requires

A probability distribution is admissible for compositional data if and only if:

  1. Its support is exactly 𝒮K−1\mathcal{S}^{K-1} (or a well-defined subset of it).
  2. It defines a proper probability measure on this space.
  3. It does not require the data to be modified before the distribution applies.

The third condition excludes models that are nominally defined on the simplex but require transformations that fail at the boundary. A model that requires adding constants to zeros, or that is undefined when any component equals zero or one, is not admissible for data that include such values.

These conditions are minimal. They say nothing about whether a model is useful, flexible, or estimable. Only whether the model is coherent with the data it purports to describe.

The Dirichlet family

The Dirichlet distribution is the canonical probability distribution on the simplex. For a composition 𝐲∈𝒮K−1\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{S}^{K-1}, the Dirichlet density with concentration parameters 𝛂=(α1,…,αK)\boldsymbol{\alpha} = (\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_K), where αk>0\alpha_k > 0, is:

p(𝐲∣𝛂)=Γ(∑k=1Kαk)∏k=1KΓ(αk)∏k=1Kykαk−1 p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \frac{\Gamma\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \alpha_k\right)}{\prod_{k=1}^{K} \Gamma(\alpha_k)} \prod_{k=1}^{K} y_k^{\alpha_k - 1}

The Dirichlet is admissible. Defined natively on the constrained space, no transformation needed. Its behaviour near the simplex boundary depends on the concentration parameters: when αk<1\alpha_k < 1, the density is unbounded as yk→0y_k \to 0, concentrating mass near the vertices and edges of the simplex; when αk=1\alpha_k = 1, the distribution is uniform; when αk>1\alpha_k > 1, the density vanishes at the boundary, concentrating mass in the interior. This flexibility allows the Dirichlet to represent compositions that tend toward sparse configurations (few dominant components) or toward balanced configurations (mass spread across components).

The Dirichlet encodes specific assumptions about dependence. Components are negatively correlated, but the correlation structure is constrained: the correlation between any two components yiy_i and yjy_j is determined entirely by the concentration parameters and is always negative. No freedom to specify arbitrary pairwise correlations. The covariance matrix of a Dirichlet-distributed vector has rank K−1K-1, reflecting the sum constraint, and its off-diagonal elements are all negative.

A strong structural assumption. The Dirichlet assumes that all dependence among components arises from the constraint and from a single shared precision parameter (the sum of concentrations). Components that share a simplex but have more complex relationships (pairs that are more or less strongly coupled than the Dirichlet permits) cannot be represented.

The logistic-normal family

The logistic-normal distribution offers a different parameterisation. It models compositions by assuming that log-ratios of components follow a multivariate normal distribution. Several equivalent formulations exist. The additive log-ratio (alr) representation selects one component as reference and models the log-ratios relative to it; the centred log-ratio (clr) uses the geometric mean as reference; the isometric log-ratio (ilr) constructs an orthonormal basis in log-ratio space. Different coordinate systems for the same family of distributions.

In the alr formulation, if 𝐲∈𝒮K−1\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{S}^{K-1} and we define 𝐳=(log⁡(y1/yK),…,log⁡(yK−1/yK))\mathbf{z} = (\log(y_1/y_K), \ldots, \log(y_{K-1}/y_K)) using the KK-th component as reference, then the logistic-normal assumes 𝐳∼𝒩(𝛍,𝚺)\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) for some mean vector 𝛍\boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}. The choice of reference component is arbitrary and does not affect the distribution on the simplex, only the parameterisation.

The logistic-normal is admissible in a restricted sense. It defines a proper distribution on the interior of the simplex, 𝒮∘K−1={𝐲:yk>0 for all k}\mathcal{S}^{K-1}_\circ = \{\mathbf{y} : y_k > 0 \text{ for all } k\}. It assigns zero probability to the boundary: any composition where at least one component is exactly zero.

A serious limitation for cover data. Structural zeros are often the majority of observations. A model that assigns zero probability to exact zeros cannot represent the data-generating process. It treats a central feature of the data as impossible.

Within its domain, the logistic-normal permits more flexible covariance structures than the Dirichlet. The matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} can encode arbitrary correlations among log-ratios, allowing components to be more or less tightly coupled than the Dirichlet would permit. Valuable when ecological or observational processes induce non-exchangeable dependence.

But this flexibility operates only on compositions without zeros. For data with structural zeros, the logistic-normal is inadmissible as a complete model.

Transformation-based approaches

Many analyses of compositional data proceed by transforming the data to an unconstrained space, fitting a standard model (typically Gaussian), and interpreting results on the original scale. Common transformations include the additive log-ratio (alr), centred log-ratio (clr), and isometric log-ratio (ilr).

These approaches are not admissible models for cover data. They fail on two grounds.

First, all log-ratio transformations are undefined at zero. A composition with any yk=0y_k = 0 cannot be transformed. The standard remedy (adding a small constant before transformation) changes the data. The resulting analysis is not an analysis of the observed composition but of a perturbed version. The perturbation is arbitrary, and results can depend on the constant chosen.

Second, fitting a Gaussian model to transformed compositions and back-transforming does not yield a valid distribution on the simplex. The Gaussian places positive probability on the entire real line. Back-transformation maps some of this probability to impossible compositions: negative proportions, proportions exceeding one, or vectors that do not sum to one. The resulting “distribution” on the original scale is not a probability distribution at all.

These approaches may produce numbers. They do not produce valid probabilistic statements about compositions.

What geometry forces

The simplex geometry constrains not just which distributions are admissible, but what their covariance structures can look like.

Any random vector 𝐲\mathbf{y} on 𝒮K−1\mathcal{S}^{K-1} must satisfy ∑kyk=1\sum_k y_k = 1 with probability one. This implies that the covariance matrix Cov(𝐲)\text{Cov}(\mathbf{y}) is singular: rank at most K−1K-1. Rows and columns sum to zero. The constraint forces this property; it does not arise from specific distributional choices.

Not all covariance matrices with this structure are achievable. The matrix must be consistent with the non-negativity constraints yk≥0y_k \geq 0. Consider a simple example: if K=3K = 3 and one component has very high variance while the others have low variance, the high-variance component would frequently take values outside [0,1][0, 1] unless the covariances are carefully calibrated. More generally, variances near the boundary of the simplex are constrained by how close the mean is to that boundary. A component with mean 0.05 cannot have the same variance as a component with mean 0.50 without violating the non-negativity constraint.

The space of valid covariance matrices for compositions is smaller than it might appear. Specifying an arbitrary (K−1)×(K−1)(K-1) \times (K-1) covariance matrix for log-ratios, or an arbitrary K×KK \times K covariance matrix for proportions, does not guarantee that a corresponding distribution exists on the simplex. Model specification must respect these geometric limits.

What remains optional

Within the class of admissible models, genuine choices remain:

The form of marginal distributions. The Dirichlet implies Beta marginals for individual components. Other admissible distributions on the simplex can produce different marginal shapes: more or less peaked, more or less skewed near the boundaries.

The dependence structure beyond the constraint. The sum constraint forces some dependence, but does not determine all of it. Different admissible models encode different assumptions about how tightly components are coupled, whether some pairs are more dependent than others, and how dependence changes across the simplex.

Behaviour near boundaries. Models differ in how they treat compositions close to the simplex boundary, where one or more components are near zero or near one. Some concentrate mass in the interior; others allow mass to accumulate near edges or vertices.

These are modelling choices, not forced by geometry. But they are choices within a constrained menu. The geometry rules out most models one might naively consider; what remains is a small family with specific, identifiable assumptions.

The status of zeros

This chapter has focused on the simplex as a continuous space and on distributions defined on its interior. The treatment of exact zeros (structural absences) requires additional machinery, addressed in the next chapter.

For now, note that exact zeros create a boundary problem for any continuous distribution on the simplex. The Dirichlet can place mass near zero but not exactly at zero when αk≥1\alpha_k \geq 1; it can place mass at zero only in a limiting sense when αk<1\alpha_k < 1. The logistic-normal excludes zeros entirely. Neither family provides a complete model for compositions with structural zeros.

Not a minor gap. A fundamental limitation that any complete framework must address.

Summary

The requirement that probability models respect the simplex geometry is a hard constraint that eliminates most familiar modelling options.

Gaussian models on raw or transformed compositions are inadmissible. They place probability outside the feasible space.

Log-ratio transformations require modifying data with zeros. The modifications are arbitrary and change what is being modelled.

The Dirichlet and logistic-normal families are admissible on the simplex interior, but encode specific assumptions about dependence. The Dirichlet permits only the dependence induced by shared concentration. The logistic-normal permits flexible log-ratio covariance but assigns zero probability to compositions with zeros.

Any valid model for cover data must be defined on the simplex, assign probability only to feasible compositions, and handle structural zeros without requiring data modification. The space of such models is small. This clarifies what honest modelling requires.
